overview.title: 📖 Overview: Sharpening Rav Giddel's Rule on Piggul and Sprinkling
overview.subtitle: Meilah 4a–4b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל שֶׁהָיְתָה לָהּ שְׁעַת הֶיתֵּר לַכֹּהֲנִים – אֵין מוֹעֲלִין בָּהּ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara continues testing Rav Giddel's rule that piggul intent at sprinkling does not remove offerings of the most sacred order from me'ilah, and does not create me'ilah for offerings of lesser sanctity. Ravina raises a challenge from Ilfa's explanation of a mishna about two consecutive improper intentions, which Rav Ashi resolves by noting that piggul status is only revealed once the blood is sprinkled. The Gemara then works through several rounds of a baraita, probing each clause — including a case where blood is left overnight and sprinkled the next day — to see whether it supports or contradicts Rav Giddel. The daf closes by returning to Rabbi Yehoshua's mishna and bar Kappara's question to his nephew bar Pedat about what exactly 'a period of fitness for the priests' means.

slides.title: 🐑 Ravina's Challenge: Can Slaughter Alone Create Piggul?
slides.subtitle: Ilfa's reading of the two-rites dispute (Zevaḥim 29b) tested against Rav Giddel

nodes.content: ❓ Ilfa: the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis is about intent in TWO different rites — e.g. slaughtering one organ with 'beyond its time' intent, the second with 'outside its place' intent
⚡ Ravina to Rav Ashi: this implies slaughter ALONE with piggul intent already renders the offering piggul — contradicting Rav Giddel!
✅ Rav Ashi: Rav Giddel agrees — but the piggul status is only revealed once the blood is sprinkled, showing whether the two intents were in one rite or two
🔄 Challenge returns: if so, the thanks-offering loaves (3b) should also stay unsanctified until sprinkling — yet the mishna states 'the loaves are sanctified' from slaughter alone!

callout.label: Resolution ahead:
callout.text: The next slide explains that 'sanctified' there means something more limited than full me'ilah status.

slides.title: 🍞 What Does 'The Loaves Are Sanctified' Actually Mean?
slides.subtitle: Resolving the thanks-offering difficulty
slides.label: The answer:
slides.text: When the mishna says the loaves of a thanks offering slaughtered chutz lizmano or chutz limkomo are 'sanctified,' it does not mean they become subject to full me'ilah. It means only that they are sanctified enough to become disqualified — requiring burning rather than simply being treated as ordinary bread. This softer meaning of 'sanctified' removes the difficulty for Rav Giddel: slaughter alone with piggul intent can cause this lesser consequence without yet creating full me'ilah, which still awaits the sprinkling.

slides.title: ⚖️ Testing a Baraita Against Rav Giddel's Rule
slides.subtitle: Round by round, does each clause prove or disprove his opinion?
rows: Even after sprinkling with piggul intent, me'ilah remains — against Rav Giddel
Rejected: may mean only before sprinkling, or refer to a burnt offering (always fully God's regardless)
'If blood left overnight, then sprinkled next day — still me'ilah' (referring to a sin offering)
Sprinkling doesn't remove me'ilah when the blood itself was invalid
True, but leaving overnight is an action; piggul is only a thought — sprinkling might work differently for each
'Sacred-order piggul offering — subject to me'ilah' (before specifying, contrasted with kodashim kalim, which are never subject)
Should have split sacred-order cases into before/after sprinkling if that distinction mattered — but it didn't
This certainly supports Rav Giddel: after sprinkling, sacred-order piggul is NOT subject to me'ilah
Does the first ruling ('always subject') also support Rav Giddel by extension?
If the second clause helps him, maybe the first does too
No — the kodashim kalim ruling is unconditionally clear-cut, so its phrasing doesn't tell us anything about the sacred-order case

slides.title: 🌙 Overnight Blood vs. Piggul Intent
slides.subtitle: Why an action (linah) and a thought (piggul) may behave differently

boxes.title: Blood Left Overnight (לינה)
items: A physical failure to act properly
Later sprinkling does NOT remove the offering from me'ilah
Applies clearly to a sin offering, whose sprinkling would otherwise have permitted priestly consumption

boxes.title: Piggul Intent (מַחְשָׁבָה)
items: A disqualifying thought, not a physical defect
Sprinkling MAY be effective to remove the offering from me'ilah
This is exactly Rav Giddel's position for offerings of the most sacred order

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: The Gemara uses this distinction to explain why the overnight-blood baraita does not automatically prove or disprove Rav Giddel's rule about piggul.

slides.title: 📏 Bar Kappara's Homework Question for Bar Pedat
slides.subtitle: What did Rabbi Yehoshua mean by 'a period of fitness for the priests'?

lines.speaker: Bar Kappara
lines.text: My sister's son, think carefully about tomorrow's question in the study hall: Rabbi Yehoshua taught that an offering with 'a period of fitness for the priests' is exempt from me'ilah once disqualified.

lines.speaker: Bar Kappara
lines.text: Did we learn this about fitness of the slaughter alone — that as long as it was slaughtered properly, later disqualification exempts it from me'ilah?

lines.speaker: Setup
lines.text: The mishna's examples — notar, impurity, leaving the courtyard — all occur only after the offering was already fully and properly sacrificed, permitted to the priests.

lines.speaker: Open question
lines.text: Or does 'a period of fitness' require that the entire sacrificial process, through sprinkling, was completed properly — not slaughter alone?

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: This distinction is exactly what's at stake in the piggul cases just discussed — whether a valid slaughter alone can start the clock on 'fitness for the priests,' even if the blood is later sprinkled with disqualifying intent.

summary.principle: Piggul status and its effect on me'ilah are only fixed at the sprinkling stage — slaughter with improper intent alone can create a lesser disqualification (like the thanks-offering loaves needing burning) without yet triggering or removing full me'ilah.

flowSteps.content: 🐑 Ravina's challenge: does slaughter alone with piggul intent make an offering piggul?
✅ Rav Ashi: piggul status is only revealed at sprinkling, even though Rav Giddel maintains slaughter alone doesn't create full piggul
🍞 Thanks-offering loaves 'sanctified' from slaughter alone = only sanctified enough to require burning, not full me'ilah

columns.content: ⚖️ Baraita's second clause certainly supports Rav Giddel: post-sprinkling piggul in sacred-order offerings is exempt
🌙 Overnight blood (a physical defect) still carries me'ilah even after later sprinkling — unlike piggul (a thought)

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: an action-based disqualification (linah) survives sprinkling for me'ilah purposes; a thought-based one (piggul) may not

quiz.q: What challenge does Ravina raise to Rav Giddel's rule, based on Ilfa's explanation of the mishna in Zevaḥim 29b?
o: That sin offerings can never become piggul
That Ilfa's case seems to show that slaughter alone with piggul intent already renders an offering piggul
That Ilfa's ruling only applies to meal offerings
That the mishna in Zevaḥim contradicts the mishna in Meilah entirely
quiz.e: Ravina points out that Ilfa's example — two different intents during two different rites (slaughtering two organs) — suggests that slaughter with piggul intent alone can create piggul, seemingly contradicting Rav Giddel.

quiz.q: How does Rav Ashi resolve Ravina's challenge?
o: He says Ilfa's ruling is incorrect
He explains that piggul status is only fully revealed once the blood is sprinkled, even if the deciding intents occurred at slaughter
He says the mishna in Zevaḥim does not apply to animal offerings
He retracts Rav Giddel's opinion entirely
quiz.e: Rav Ashi maintains that whether the offering is piggul (from two rites) or not (from one rite) only becomes clear once the blood is sprinkled — consistent with Rav Giddel's view that sprinkling is what fixes the offering's status.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's resolution, what does it mean when the mishna says the thanks offering's loaves are 'sanctified' after the animal was slaughtered chutz lizmano/limkomo?
o: That they are fully subject to me'ilah like consecrated animals
That they are sanctified enough to become disqualified and require burning, not that they carry full me'ilah
That they may be eaten by non-priests
That they become permanently forbidden to everyone including priests
quiz.e: The Gemara explains 'sanctified' here in a limited sense — enough that the loaves can become disqualified and need burning — resolving the apparent conflict with Rav Giddel's rule.

quiz.q: Which clause of the tested baraita does the Gemara conclude 'certainly supports' Rav Giddel's opinion?
o: The clause stating piggul offerings are always subject to me'ilah

The clause distinguishing offerings of the most sacred order (subject to me'ilah) from offerings of lesser sanctity (never subject), without further dividing the sacred-order case by before/after sprinkling
The clause about a burnt offering
None of the clauses support him
quiz.e: Since the baraita didn't further split the sacred-order case into before/after sprinkling, the Gemara concludes it must be because after sprinkling with piggul intent, sacred-order offerings are indeed exempt from me'ilah — supporting Rav Giddel.

quiz.q: Why might sprinkling blood after piggul intent remove an offering from me'ilah, while sprinkling blood that was left overnight does not?
o: Because piggul only applies to meal offerings
Because leaving blood overnight is a physical defect (an action), while piggul is only a disqualifying thought, and the two may be treated differently regarding sprinkling's effect
Because overnight blood can never be sprinkled at all
Because piggul offerings cannot have their blood sprinkled
quiz.e: The Gemara distinguishes: linah (leaving blood overnight) is an action-based disqualification that sprinkling cannot cure for me'ilah purposes, whereas piggul is a thought-based disqualification, where sprinkling may still be effective to remove the offering from me'ilah.
